name: Ketone monoester (R-1,3-butanediol ester)

lead: The ketone monoester is a drink that quickly raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate. It was developed at the NIH and sold under brands such as KetoneAid, and people use it for appetite control and fat loss on the way to a leaner body.

It is broken down into ketone bodies the body can use as fuel, raising blood ketones without fasting or dieting. It is the best-studied exogenous ketone, with human studies on kinetics, endurance and appetite, including one report of lower ghrelin and appetite. Fat loss and appearance have not been tested in published trials found here.

paras: It is drunk as a liquid, often around training or between meals to blunt hunger, and used alongside a low-carb or calorie-controlled diet.
The 2012 study reported on tolerability in healthy adults. Long-term effects in healthy dieters are not established.

angle.text: The ketone monoester drink raises blood ketones quickly, and the appearance interest is appetite control: one study found lower appetite hormones, which could help you eat less and get leaner. Fat-loss trial results are not published.

lead: The ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate is a drink that raises blood D-beta-hydroxybutyrate (a ketone body) within an hour or so, without fasting or a ketogenic diet. In body-composition circles it is discussed as a way to reach ketosis and to blunt hunger, which could support staying in a calorie deficit and so a leaner-looking physique; the athletes who use it say they do so for endurance fuel. It was developed at the US National Institutes of Health by Richard Veech and Todd King and later sold by companies including KetoneAid, TDeltaS and HVMN, according to Wikipedia.[1]

It is the most-researched exogenous ketone. Human studies have examined its kinetics and tolerability, how it compares with ketone salts, its effects on fuel use in athletes, its effect on appetite hormones, and its effect on brain network stability.[2][3][4][5][6] In the appetite study, 15 normal-weight adults who drank the ester after an overnight fast had lower ghrelin, insulin, GLP-1 and PYY in the following hours than after an equal-calorie dextrose drink, along with lower reported hunger.[5]

No published trial has tested the ketone monoester for fat loss or physical appearance; the appetite finding comes from a single acute study in lean volunteers. Registered trials are now examining it in heart failure, kidney disease, ageing and other settings.[7][8][9][10][11][12]

Sold as a dietary or sports supplement; not an approved medicine

paras: Exogenous ketones are ketone bodies taken as supplements. Most use beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), which the body also makes in the liver during fasting, ketogenic diets and prolonged exercise, and which is converted to acetoacetate and then acetyl-CoA to feed the Krebs cycle.[1] Wikipedia notes that BHB is technically an acid rather than a ketone but behaves like one in metabolism.[1]

Wikipedia describes the main forms as ketone salts (BHB bound to sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium, usually as a racemic mix in which only the D-isomer is readily used), the monoester (BHB linked to D-1,3-butanediol, fermentation-derived), a triglyceride form, an acetoacetate diester tested in deep-sea divers, a newer diester sold with food, and R-1,3-butanediol itself, which the article says is not the same as 1,4-butanediol.[1] Esters are described as more than 99 percent D-isomer, while salts contain roughly half of the slower-metabolised L-isomer.[1]

The monoester is a liquid that, per Wikipedia, is digested quickly with the liver releasing the remainder more slowly.[1] Users take it as a drink; products are sold as sports and nutrition supplements.

In the 2012 study, healthy volunteers drank the monoester in a meal-replacement beverage at three single-dose levels. Plasma BHB and acetoacetate rose, the intact ester was not detected in blood, and peak ketone levels were reached in one to two hours, with BHB reaching 3.30 mM and acetoacetate 1.19 mM at the highest dose. The elimination half-life was 0.8 to 3.1 hours for BHB and 8 to 14 hours for acetoacetate.[2] The same paper ran a five-day, three-times-daily phase and reported general tolerability, with some gastrointestinal effects when large volumes of the milk-based drink were consumed at the highest dose; the authors concluded it was a simple way to raise blood ketones compared with preparing a ketogenic diet.[2]

A 2017 set of three randomised studies compared the ester with ketone salts, tested the effect of a meal, and examined a nine-hour ester regimen. With drinks delivering about 12 or 24 g of BHB, mean peak D-BHB was 2.8 mM for the ester and 1.0 mM for the salts, which returned to baseline within three to four hours; a meal lowered the ester's peak by about a third, and all ketone drinks lowered blood glucose, free fatty acids and triglycerides. The authors concluded exogenous ketone drinks are a practical way to achieve ketosis.[3]

Wikipedia notes that, unlike salts, esters lower blood pH through hepatic metabolism, and that ketones reduce peripheral glucose use, have anti-lipolytic effects on fat tissue and reduce muscle protein breakdown.[1] It also describes ketones as limiting liver glucose production and lowering blood glucose.[1]

The monoester came out of work at the US National Institutes of Health by Richard Veech and Todd King, according to Wikipedia; it was later commercialised by several companies.[1] Veech, King and Kieran Clarke are all authors of the 2012 kinetics paper, and Clarke, Veech and King are also among the authors of the 2016 athlete paper.[2][4]

The kinetic and tolerability paper appeared in 2012,[2] and the 2016 report described studies in elite athletes.[4] The mouse and case-report literature includes a 2013 study of a ketone ester diet in an Alzheimer's mouse model, a 2014 study of ketone supplementation in mice with metastatic cancer and a 2015 case report in one Alzheimer's patient.[13][14][15]
Wikipedia cites a November 2017 article in The Atlantic among the popular-press coverage of the products.[1]

The 2016 paper in Cell Metabolism reported five studies in 39 high-performance athletes and described ketosis from the ester as decreasing muscle glycolysis and plasma lactate, increasing intramuscular triacylglycerol oxidation during exercise, and providing an alternative substrate for oxidative phosphorylation, even with normal muscle glycogen, carbohydrate intake and raised insulin.[4] The authors framed this as a change in fuel preference that improved physical endurance.[4]

A 2018 study reported that the ester drink raised blood BHB from about 0.2 to 3.3 mM within an hour and lowered ghrelin and appetite in humans; the authors concluded that raised blood ketones may directly suppress appetite.[5] A 2020 imaging study in 42 adults found brain network stability was lowered by glucose and raised by ketones, whether from a ketogenic diet or from a ketone ester bolus, and the authors suggested dietary approaches that increase ketone use could be explored in brain ageing.[6] Mouse studies have tested ketone esters in Alzheimer's disease and cancer models, and a single case report described use in an Alzheimer's patient.[13][14][15]

Wikipedia also reports a 2024 study of NCAA Division I cross-country athletes in which time to fatigue was not significantly different with 1,3-butanediol, a related precursor.[1] A review linking ketone bodies to the effects of caloric restriction has been published.[16]

Human studies include the pharmacokinetics and tolerability study in healthy adults,[2] the three randomised metabolic studies comparing ester and salts,[3] the five studies in 39 athletes,[4] the appetite study in 15 normal-weight adults,[5] and the 42-adult brain imaging study.[6] Registered trials include ketone esters in heart failure, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, polycystic kidney disease, ageing and senescent T cells, nocturnal blood pressure, cerebrospinal fluid ketone levels and hypoxic tolerance.[7][8][9][10][11][12] A registered trial on ketone supplementation and postprandial lipemia in people with overweight and obesity was withdrawn.[17] No studies found on fat loss or appearance.

The monoester is sold as a supplement drink; Wikipedia lists KetoneAid, TDeltaS and HVMN among the companies that have commercialised it, and the published appearance-related data are limited to the single acute appetite study.[1][5] Supplement regulation varies by country.

The published tolerability data are from short studies in healthy adults, in which gastrointestinal effects were reported at the highest doses with a large volume of drink.[2] Long-term effects in healthy people using it for appearance goals have not been studied. Wikipedia notes that esters lower blood pH, while salts add sodium or other minerals along with BHB.[1] Product labels and the supplement market vary by country.
